claim: RIG-I distinguishes 5′ tri- or diphosphate containing viral double-stranded (ds) RNA from self-RNA by an incompletely understood mechanism that involves ATP hydrolysis by RIG-I's RNA translocase domain.
source: The cytosolic antiviral innate immune sensor RIG-I distinguishes 5′ tri- or diphosphate containing viral double-stranded (ds) RNA from self-RNA by an incompletely understood mechanism that involves ATP hydrolysis by RIG-I's RNA translocase domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about RIG-I function, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mutations in ATPase motifs can lead to the multi-system disorder Singleton-Merten Syndrome (SMS) and increased interferon levels.
source: Recently discovered mutations in ATPase motifs can lead to the multi-system disorder Singleton-Merten Syndrome (SMS) and increased interferon levels, suggesting misregulated signaling by RIG-I.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research linking SMS to RIG-I mutations, as referenced in the introduction section.

claim: SMS mutations phenocopy a mutation that allows ATP binding but prevents hydrolysis.
source: Here we report that SMS mutations phenocopy a mutation that allows ATP binding but prevents hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data comparing SMS mutations to the E373Q mutation.

claim: ATPase deficient RIG-I constitutively signals through endogenous RNA.
source: ATPase deficient RIG-I constitutively signals through endogenous RNA and co-purifies with self-RNA even from virus infected cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase assays showing signaling in non-infected cells and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: ATPase deficient RIG-I co-purifies with self-RNA even from virus infected cells.
source: ATPase deficient RIG-I constitutively signals through endogenous RNA and co-purifies with self-RNA even from virus infected cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments from infected cells showing RNA binding.

claim: A 60S ribosomal expansion segment is a dominant self-RNA that is stably bound by ATPase deficient RIG-I.
source: Biochemical studies and cryo-electron microscopy identify a 60S ribosomal expansion segment as a dominant self-RNA that is stably bound by ATPase deficient RIG-I.
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and biochemical binding assays showing interaction with ribosomal RNA.

claim: ATP hydrolysis displaces wild-type RIG-I from self-RNA but not from 5' triphosphate dsRNA.
source: ATP hydrolysis displaces wild-type RIG-I from this self-RNA but not from 5' triphosphate dsRNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA and fluorescence anisotropy experiments showing differential effects of ATP on binding to different RNA substrates.

claim: ATP-hydrolysis prevents recognition of self-RNA.
source: Our results indicate that ATP-hydrolysis prevents recognition of self-RNA and suggest that SMS mutations lead to unintentional signaling through prolonged RNA binding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased self-RNA binding by ATPase-deficient mutants.

claim: SMS mutations lead to unintentional signaling through prolonged RNA binding.
source: Our results indicate that ATP-hydrolysis prevents recognition of self-RNA and suggest that SMS mutations lead to unintentional signaling through prolonged RNA binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SMS mutations phenocopy ATP hydrolysis-deficient mutants that show prolonged RNA binding and constitutive signaling.

claim: RIG-I senses RNA from a broad range of viruses including measles virus and Sendai virus (both paramyxoviridae), Influenza A virus, Japanese encephalitis virus and Hepatitis C virus.
source: RIG-I senses RNA from a broad range of viruses including measles virus and Sendai virus (both paramyxoviridae), Influenza A virus, Japanese encephalitis virus and Hepatitis C virus, whereas MDA5 is activated for example by picornavirus RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, as indicated by the context in the introduction.

claim: MDA5 is activated by picornavirus RNA.
source: RIG-I senses RNA from a broad range of viruses including measles virus and Sendai virus (both paramyxoviridae), Influenza A virus, Japanese encephalitis virus and Hepatitis C virus, whereas MDA5 is activated for example by picornavirus RNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about MDA5 specificity.

claim: RIG-I preferentially detects base-paired double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) ends containing either 5′ triphosphate (ppp) or 5′ diphosphate (pp) moieties.
source: RIG-I preferentially detects base-paired double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) ends containing either 5′ triphosphate (ppp) or 5′ diphosphate (pp) moieties (Goubau et al., 2014; Hornung et al., 2006; Pichlmair et al., 2006; Schlee et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009) and not 2' OH methylated at the first 5' terminal nucleotide (Schuberth-Wagner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing RIG-I ligand specificity.

claim: RIG-I does not detect RNA that is 2' OH methylated at the first 5' terminal nucleotide.
source: RIG-I preferentially detects base-paired double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) ends containing either 5′ triphosphate (ppp) or 5′ diphosphate (pp) moieties (Goubau et al., 2014; Hornung et al., 2006; Pichlmair et al., 2006; Schlee et al., 2009; Schmidt et al., 2009) and not 2' OH methylated at the first 5' terminal nucleotide (Schuberth-Wagner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on RNA modifications affecting RIG-I recognition.

claim: ppp-dsRNA arises at panhandle structures of influenza virus nucleocapsids, or during measles or Sendai virus transcription.
source: ppp-dsRNA arises, for example, at panhandle structures of influenza virus nucleocapsids, or during measles or Sendai virus transcription (Liu et al., 2015; Weber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on viral RNA structures.

claim: 5′ diphosphates are found on genomic RNA of reoviruses.
source: 5′ diphosphates are found on genomic RNA of reoviruses (Banerjee and Shatkin, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on reovirus RNA structure.

claim: RIG-I can detect poly-U/UC-rich dsRNA.
source: RIG-I can also detect poly-U/UC-rich dsRNA (Schnell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on RIG-I ligand specificity.

claim: Ligands of MDA5 include dsRNA longer than 1000 bp.
source: Ligands of MDA5 are less well characterized but include dsRNA longer than 1000 bp (Kato et al., 2008), higher-order dsRNA structures (Pichlmair et al., 2009), or AU-rich RNA (Runge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on MDA5 ligand specificity.

claim: Ligands of MDA5 include higher-order dsRNA structures.
source: Ligands of MDA5 are less well characterized but include dsRNA longer than 1000 bp (Kato et al., 2008), higher-order dsRNA structures (Pichlmair et al., 2009), or AU-rich RNA (Runge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on MDA5 ligand specificity.

claim: Ligands of MDA5 include AU-rich RNA.
source: Ligands of MDA5 are less well characterized but include dsRNA longer than 1000 bp (Kato et al., 2008), higher-order dsRNA structures (Pichlmair et al., 2009), or AU-rich RNA (Runge et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on MDA5 ligand specificity.

claim: RIG-I and MDA5 consist of two N-terminal tandem caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD), a central ATPase/translocase domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain (RD).
source: RIG-I and MDA5 consist of two N-terminal tandem caspase activation and recruitment domains (2CARD), a central ATPase/translocase domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain (RD).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about RLR domain architecture.

claim: LGP2 lacks the 2CARD module but otherwise has a similar domain architecture to RIG-I and MDA5.
source: LGP2 lacks the 2CARD module but otherwise has a similar domain architecture.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about LGP2.

claim: Binding of RNA induces a conformational change in RIG-I.
source: Binding of RNA induces a conformational change in RIG-I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RIG-I activation mechanism.

claim: When activated, the RD binds the ppp- or pp-dsRNA end, while the SF2 domain interacts with the adjacent RNA duplex and forms an active ATPase site.
source: If activated, the RD binds the ppp- or pp-dsRNA end, while the SF2 domain interacts with the adjacent RNA duplex and forms an active ATPase site (Civril et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of RIG-I.

claim: In the activated conformation, the 2CARD module is sterically displaced from its auto-inhibited state.
source: In this conformation, the 2CARD module is sterically displaced from its auto-inhibited state (Jiang et al., 2011; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2011) and can be K63-linked poly-ubiquitinated (Gack et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies showing conformational changes.

claim: The 2CARD module can be K63-linked poly-ubiquitinated upon RIG-I activation.
source: In this conformation, the 2CARD module is sterically displaced from its auto-inhibited state (Jiang et al., 2011; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Luo et al., 2011) and can be K63-linked poly-ubiquitinated (Gack et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on RIG-I post-translational modifications.

claim: Multiple Ub-2CARD complexes assemble to form a nucleation site for the polymerization of MAVS into long helical filaments.
source: Multiple Ub-2CARD complexes assemble to form a nucleation site for the polymerization of mitochondrial antiviral-signaling adaptor protein (MAVS) into long helical filaments (Hou et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on MAVS activation mechanism.

claim: MDA5 cooperatively polymerizes along dsRNA instead of recognizing terminal structures like RIG-I.
source: Instead of recognizing terminal structures like RIG-I, MDA5 cooperatively polymerizes along dsRNA (Berke and Modis, 2012), which is suggested to trigger MAVS polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on MDA5 mechanism.

claim: MDA5 polymerization along dsRNA is suggested to trigger MAVS polymerization.
source: Instead of recognizing terminal structures like RIG-I, MDA5 cooperatively polymerizes along dsRNA (Berke and Modis, 2012), which is suggested to trigger MAVS polymerization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior research, as indicated by 'suggested'.

claim: Mutation of the seven SF2 'helicase' motifs resulted in RLRs that are either inactive or signal constitutively.
source: Mutation of the seven SF2 "helicase" motifs resulted in RLRs that are either inactive or signal constitutively (Bamming and Horvath, 2009; Louber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mutational studies.

claim: Overexpression of the 2CARD module alone is sufficient for signaling.
source: On the other hand, overexpression of the 2CARD module alone is sufficient for signaling (Yoneyama et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on RIG-I signaling.

claim: The SF2 domain is an ATP-dependent dsRNA translocase.
source: Further studies revealed that the SF2 domain is an ATP-dependent dsRNA translocase (Myong et al., 2009) that can help enhance signaling by loading multiple RIG-I on dsRNA (Patel et al., 2013) and may execute anti-viral "effector" functions through displacement of viral proteins (Yao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior biochemical studies.

claim: The SF2 domain can help enhance signaling by loading multiple RIG-I on dsRNA.
source: Further studies revealed that the SF2 domain is an ATP-dependent dsRNA translocase (Myong et al., 2009) that can help enhance signaling by loading multiple RIG-I on dsRNA (Patel et al., 2013) and may execute anti-viral "effector" functions through displacement of viral proteins (Yao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research on RIG-I mechanism.

claim: The SF2 domain may execute anti-viral 'effector' functions through displacement of viral proteins.
source: Further studies revealed that the SF2 domain is an ATP-dependent dsRNA translocase (Myong et al., 2009) that can help enhance signaling by loading multiple RIG-I on dsRNA (Patel et al., 2013) and may execute anti-viral "effector" functions through displacement of viral proteins (Yao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation, as indicated by 'may'.

claim: RIG-I ATPase activity promotes recycling of RIG-I:dsRNA complexes in vitro, suggesting a kinetic discrimination between self and non-self RNA.
source: Finally, RIG-I ATPase activity promotes recycling of RIG-I:dsRNA complexes in vitro, suggesting a kinetic discrimination between self and non-self RNA (Anchisi et al., 2015; Louber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies, with the discrimination mechanism being an inference.

claim: Several autoimmune diseases, including the Aicardi-Goutières and Singleton-Merten syndromes (SMS), were linked to single amino acid mutations in the SF2 domains of MDA5 and RIG-I.
source: Several autoimmune diseases, including the Aicardi-Goutières and Singleton-Merten syndromes (SMS), were linked to single amino acid mutations in the SF2 domains of MDA5 and RIG-I (Funabiki et al., 2014; Jang et al., 2015; Rice et al., 2014; Rutsch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: Two point mutations within the Walker A (motif I) or Walker B (motif II) of RIG-I are linked to atypical SMS.
source: Two point mutations within the Walker A (motif I) or Walker B (motif II) of RIG-I are linked to atypical SMS and functional studies indicated constitutive RIG-I activation (Jang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior genetic and functional studies.

claim: Functional studies indicated constitutive RIG-I activation in SMS mutations.
source: Two point mutations within the Walker A (motif I) or Walker B (motif II) of RIG-I are linked to atypical SMS and functional studies indicated constitutive RIG-I activation (Jang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior functional studies.

claim: Previous mutations in motif I led to loss of RIG-I function.
source: Thus, these mutations have been described as a gain of function, which is puzzling considering previous mutations in motif I led to loss of RIG-I function, while mutations in motif II led to either gain or loss of function, depending on the type of mutation (Bamming and Horvath, 2009; Louber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mutational studies.

claim: Previous mutations in motif II led to either gain or loss of function, depending on the type of mutation.
source: Thus, these mutations have been described as a gain of function, which is puzzling considering previous mutations in motif I led to loss of RIG-I function, while mutations in motif II led to either gain or loss of function, depending on the type of mutation (Bamming and Horvath, 2009; Louber et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior mutational studies.

claim: Overexpressed wild-type RIG-I is able to induce a slight activation of the IFNβ promoter.
source: Overexpressed wild-type RIG-I (wtRIG-I) is able to induce a slight activation of the IFNβ promoter, which can be further amplified by stimulation with Sendai virus defective interfering particles (SeV DIs) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Wild-type RIG-I activation can be further amplified by stimulation with Sendai virus defective interfering particles (SeV DIs).
source: Overexpressed wild-type RIG-I (wtRIG-I) is able to induce a slight activation of the IFNβ promoter, which can be further amplified by stimulation with Sendai virus defective interfering particles (SeV DIs) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 2CARD module (RIG-I 1-229) induced a strong activation in both non-infected and SeV DI-stimulated cells.
source: The 2CARD module (RIG-I 1-229) induced a strong activation in both non-infected and SeV DI-stimulated cells and is crucial since constructs lacking these domains (Δ2CARD, RIG-I 230-925) cannot conduct any downstream signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Constructs lacking the 2CARD domains (Δ2CARD, RIG-I 230-925) cannot conduct any downstream signaling.
source: The 2CARD module (RIG-I 1-229) induced a strong activation in both non-infected and SeV DI-stimulated cells and is crucial since constructs lacking these domains (Δ2CARD, RIG-I 230-925) cannot conduct any downstream signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RIG-I K270I, carrying a mutation in the motif I lysine that reduces ATP binding, signaled in neither uninfected nor SeV DIs stimulated cells.
source: RIG-I K270I, carrying a mutation in the motif I lysine that reduces ATP binding (Rozen et al., 1989), signaled in neither uninfected nor SeV DIs stimulated cells, consistent with previous studies.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: RIG-I E373Q, which has a stabilized ATP-bound state by slowed-down ATP hydrolysis, strongly signaled in both non-infected and SeV DIs stimulated cells.
source: Remarkably, the E373Q substitution in motif II had a strikingly different effect. RIG E373Q, which has a stabilized ATP-bound state by slowed-down ATP hydrolysis, strongly signaled in both non-infected and SeV DIs stimulated cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RIG-I and RIG-I E373Q have the same solution structure.
source: To rule out a "constitutive" active conformation of RIG-I E373Q due to an exposed 2CARD module (e.g. from an unfolded SF2) we performed small angle X-ray scattering with purified wtRIG-I and RIG-I E373Q demonstrating that both proteins have the same solution structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SAXS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The E373Q mutation does not destabilize RIG-I.
source: In addition, thermal unfolding assays show that the E373Q mutation does not destabilize RIG-I (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: RIG-I Δ2CARD,E373Q has a dominant negative effect on signaling by RIG-I E373Q.
source: Finally, RIG-I Δ2CARD,E373Q has a dominant negative effect on signaling by RIG-I E373Q (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: RIG-I E373Q is neither destabilized nor constitutively active, suggesting it needs productive RNA interactions.
source: Taken together, these data show that RIG-I E373Q is neither destabilized nor constitutively active, suggesting it needs productive RNA interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the SAXS, thermal shift, and dominant negative data.

claim: The single mutation RIG-I T347A did not signal in either infected or non-infected cells.
source: The single mutation RIG-I T347A did not signal in either infected or non-infected cells, showing that the interaction of RNA with this specific amino acid is critical for signaling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The interaction of RNA with T347 is critical for RIG-I signaling.
source: The single mutation RIG-I T347A did not signal in either infected or non-infected cells, showing that the interaction of RNA with this specific amino acid is critical for signaling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of signaling in the T347A mutant.

claim: The single mutation V699A slightly increases the signaling activity of RIG-I in non-infected cells.
source: Interestingly, we find that the single mutation V699A slightly increases the signaling activity of RIG-I in non-infected cells (Figure 1C), which could be explained by a putative reduction of translocation activity instead of a prevention of RNA binding to SF2 (see discussion).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of the regulatory domain (ΔRD) inactivates signaling in both infected and non-infected cells.
source: Finally, deletion of the regulatory domain (ΔRD) inactivates signaling in both infected and non-infected cells as previously observed (Cui et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Both combination mutants RIG-I E373Q,T347A and RIG-I E373Q,ΔRD failed to signal in both SeV DIs infected and non-infected cells.
source: As expected, both combination mutants RIG-I E373Q,T347A and RIG-I E373Q,ΔRD failed to signal in both SeV DIs infected and non-infected cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increased immunostimulatory effect of E373Q requires a productive RNA interaction of SF2 and RD.
source: These data show that the increased immunostimulatory effect of E373Q requires a productive RNA interaction of SF2 and RD.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of signaling in double mutants affecting RNA binding.

claim: K888 mediates triphosphate binding in RD.
source: K888 mediates triphosphate binding in RD and mutations in this residue inactivate recognition of viral RNA (Cui et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural and functional studies.

claim: Mutations in K888 inactivate recognition of viral RNA.
source: K888 mediates triphosphate binding in RD and mutations in this residue inactivate recognition of viral RNA (Cui et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: RIG-I E373Q,K888T is still constitutively active in non-infected cells.
source: Of note RIG-I E373Q,K888T is still constitutively active in non-infected cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increased signaling capacity of E373Q on endogenous RNA is independent from the ppp-dsRNA or pp-dsRNA epitopes that RIG-I recognizes on viral RNA via the RD.
source: This effect indicates that the increased signaling capacity on endogenous RNA is independent from the ppp-dsRNA or pp-dsRNA epitopes that RIG-I recognizes on viral RNA via the RD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the K888T mutation does not abolish constitutive signaling of E373Q.

claim: E373A leads to a constitutive activation of the IFNβ promoter.
source: E373A is at the same position as our structure-derived E373Q mutant. Consistent with this, we observed that this substitution leads to a constitutive activation of the IFNβ promoter (Jang et al., 2015) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: C268F leads to constitutive signaling.
source: Interestingly, although C268 is located in motif I, it also leads to constitutive signaling, whereas motif I mutation of K270 (which coordinates the β-phosphate of ATP) blocks ATP binding and renders RIG-I inactive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mutation of the non-ATP binding C268 in motif I appears to phenocopy a mutation that prevents ATP hydrolysis.
source: Thus, mutation of the non-ATP binding C268 in motif I appears to phenocopy a mutation that prevents ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that C268F shows similar constitutive signaling as E373Q.

claim: Signaling of RIG-I requires both ATP and RNA binding.
source: In summary, our studies show that signaling of RIG-I requires both ATP and RNA binding.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutational analysis showing that mutations affecting either ATP or RNA binding abolish signaling.

claim: ATP hydrolysis appears to be critical to dissolve the signaling state and to prevent activation of RIG-I by self-RNA.
source: ATP hydrolysis, on the other hand, appears to be critical to dissolve the signaling state and to prevent activation of RIG-I by self-RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that ATP hydrolysis-deficient mutants show constitutive signaling through self-RNA.

claim: The amount of RNA recovered from RIG-I E373Q was about 3 times higher than that from RIG-I, regardless of whether co-purified from infected or non-infected cells.
source: Regardless of whether co-purified from infected or non-infected cells, the amount of RNA recovered from RIG-I E373Q was about 3 times higher than that from RIG-I (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of co-immunoprecipitated RNA shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Increased amounts of RNA co-purified with the SMS mutants C268F and E373A from uninfected cells, reflecting the same altered RNA binding properties as in RIG-I E373Q.
source: Similarly increased amounts of RNA co-purified with the SMS mutants C268F and E373A from uninfected cells, reflecting the same altered RNA binding properties as in RIG-I E373Q (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of co-immunoprecipitated RNA shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The increased amount of RNA co-purified with RIG-I E373Q is to a large extent due to the presence of 28S rRNA, while 18S rRNA remains unaltered.
source: When analyzed on a Bioanalyzer RNA chip or on agarose gels, we found that the increased amount of RNA is to a large extent due to the presence of 28S rRNA, while 18S rRNA remains unaltered (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Bioanalyzer and gel analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The total RNA content ruled out an alteration of ribosome subunit ratio in RIG-I E373Q transfected cells.
source: Control analysis of the total RNA content ruled out an alteration of ribosome subunit ratio in RIG-I E373Q transfected cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by total RNA analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both increased amount of RNA and specific enrichment of 28S rRNA were also observed for the equivalent MDA5 E444Q Walker B mutant.
source: Both increased amount of RNA and specific enrichment of 28S rRNA were also observed for the equivalent MDA5 E444Q Walker B mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation and Bioanalyzer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: RNA co-purified with wtRIG-I and RIG-I lacking the 2CARD module induced an immune response in HEK 293T ISRE-FF/RFP reporter cells.
source: RNA co-purified with wtRIG-I and RIG-I lacking the 2CARD module induced an immune response in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RNA co-purified with RIG-I K270I (ATP binding deficient) and V699A (putative translocation deficient) was able to stimulate the ISRE reporter in an amount comparable to wtRIG-I.
source: RNA co-purified with RIG-I K270I (ATP binding deficient) and V699A (putative translocation deficient) was also able to stimulate the ISRE reporter in an amount comparable to wtRIG-I, indicating no altered RNA binding properties in these mutants under virus infected conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RNA that co-purified with the RNA-binding deficient RIG-I T347A, RIG-I K858E or RIG-I ΔRD poorly stimulated the ISRE promoter and probably represents background RNA.
source: In contrast, RNA that co-purified with the RNA-binding deficient RIG-I T347A (mutation in SF2 domain), RIG-I K858E (mutation in RD domain that reduces triphosphate recognition) or RIG-I ΔRD poorly stimulated the ISRE promoter and probably represents background RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RIG-I recognizes immunostimulatory RNA via the SF2 and RD domains, but does not require ATP binding for this process.
source: These data suggest that RIG-I recognizes immunostimulatory RNA via the SF2 and RD domains, but does not require ATP binding for this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that K270I mutant co-purifies with immunostimulatory RNA despite lacking ATP binding.

claim: RNA co-purified with RIG-I E373Q failed to induce reporter gene expression.
source: Interestingly, RNA co-purified with RIG-I E373Q failed to induce reporter gene expression (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Despite RIG-I E373Q co-purifying with approximately threefold more RNA than wtRIG-I from infected cells, the co-purified RNA is not immunostimulatory in a wtRIG-I background.
source: Thus, despite the observation that RIG-I E373Q co-purifies with approximately threefold more RNA than wtRIG-I from infected cells, the co-purified RNA is not immunostimulatory in a wtRIG-I background.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that RNA from E373Q does not stimulate reporter cells containing endogenous wtRIG-I.

claim: Cells that transiently express RIG-I E373Q can be further stimulated by transfection of total RNA extracts and purified ribosomal RNA.
source: However, cells that transiently express RIG-I E373Q can be further stimulated by transfection of total RNA extracts and purified ribosomal RNA (Figure 2E), suggesting that ribosomal RNA can activate RIG-I E373Q.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Ribosomal RNA can activate RIG-I E373Q.
source: However, cells that transiently express RIG-I E373Q can be further stimulated by transfection of total RNA extracts and purified ribosomal RNA (Figure 2E), suggesting that ribosomal RNA can activate RIG-I E373Q.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that transfection of ribosomal RNA stimulates E373Q-expressing cells.

claim: Cells lacking wtRIG-I or RIG-I E373Q do not respond to total RNA or ribosomal RNA.
source: Cells lacking wtRIG-I or RIG-I E373Q on the other hand do not respond to those RNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Host-RNA, which does not activate wtRIG-I, can apparently compete with viral RNA for RIG-I E373Q.
source: We conclude that host-RNA, which does not activate wtRIG-I, can apparently compete with viral RNA for RIG-I E373Q.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that E373Q co-purifies with non-immunostimulatory RNA even from infected cells.

claim: Both RIG-I E373Q and the wild-type protein are able to bind ATP.
source: We confirmed that while both RIG-I E373Q and the wild-type protein are able to bind ATP, only wtRIG-I can hydrolyze ATP (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by DRaCALA ATP binding assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Only wtRIG-I can hydrolyze ATP, not RIG-I E373Q.
source: We confirmed that while both RIG-I E373Q and the wild-type protein are able to bind ATP, only wtRIG-I can hydrolyze ATP (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP hydrolysis assay shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In presence of ATP a minor binding of wtRIG-I to the ribosome could be observed, whereas RIG-I E373Q bound in a near stoichiometric manner.
source: In presence of ATP a minor binding of wtRIG-I to the ribosome could be observed, whereas RIG-I E373Q bound in a near stoichiometric manner.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In absence of ATP or in presence of ADP·BeF3 binding of wtRIG-I was greatly enhanced and showed similar levels compared to RIG-I E373Q.
source: In absence of ATP or in presence of ADP·BeF3 binding of wtRIG-I was greatly enhanced and showed similar levels compared to RIG-I E373Q (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average resolution of the RIG-I E373Q:80S ribosome complex cryo-EM reconstruction was estimated to be 17.7 Å based on the Fourier shell correlation cut-off criterion at 0.5.
source: The average resolution was estimated to be 17.7 Å based on the Fourier shell correlation cut-off criterion at 0.5.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: The ribosome:RIG-I E373Q complex revealed an additional density located at rRNA expansion segment (ES) 7L, which is located at the back of the large ribosomal subunit.
source: When compared with the reconstruction of the human 80S ribosome alone (Figure 3E), the ribosome:RIG-I E373Q complex revealed an additional density located at rRNA expansion segment (ES) 7L, which is located at the back of the large ribosomal subunit.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Human ribosomes contain several long, G:C rich, base-paired RNA expansion segments forming large tentacle-like hairpin structures of substantial double-stranded nature.
source: Human ribosomes contain several long, G:C rich, base-paired RNA expansion segments forming large tentacle-like hairpin structures of substantial double-stranded nature (Anger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural studies of human ribosomes.

claim: A large part of the double-stranded RNA in ribosomal expansion segments is not covered by ribosomal proteins and accessible for cytosolic proteins.
source: A large part of the double-stranded RNA in these segments is not covered by ribosomal proteins and accessible for cytosolic proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosomal structure.

claim: The crystal structure of ADP·BeFx-bound RIG-I △2CARD:RNA complex fits well into the density observed at ES7L.
source: The crystal structure of ADP·BeFx-bound RIG-I △2CARD:RNA complex ((Jiang et al., 2011), PDB code 3TMI) fits well into the density observed at ES7L and is located at the root of the solvent exposed portion of helix A of ES7L that contains a contiguous stretch of seven G:C/C:G base pairs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by fitting of the crystal structure into the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RIG-I binds at the root of the solvent exposed portion of helix A of ES7L that contains a contiguous stretch of seven G:C/C:G base pairs.
source: The crystal structure of ADP·BeFx-bound RIG-I △2CARD:RNA complex ((Jiang et al., 2011), PDB code 3TMI) fits well into the density observed at ES7L and is located at the root of the solvent exposed portion of helix A of ES7L that contains a contiguous stretch of seven G:C/C:G base pairs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Stabilizing the ATP-bound state of RIG-I induces a conformation where RIG-I binds to ribosomes, presumably at exposed dsRNA expansion segments.
source: In summary, we conclude that stabilizing the ATP-bound state of RIG-I induces a conformation where RIG-I binds to ribosomes, presumably at exposed dsRNA expansion segments.
evidence: This is concluded from the cryo-EM and biochemical data showing ribosome binding by E373Q.

claim: RIG-I and RIG-I E373Q bound to the 24mer blunt ended dsRNA with a slightly higher affinity in presence of ATP or ADP·BeF3 than in its absence.
source: RIG-I and RIG-I E373Q bound to the 24mer blunt ended dsRNA with a slightly higher affinity in presence of ATP or ADP·BeF3 than in its absence (Figure 4A), suggesting that ATP binding to the SF2 domain positively contributes to the overall affinity in addition to RD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ATP binding to the SF2 domain positively contributes to the overall affinity for blunt-ended dsRNA in addition to RD.
source: RIG-I and RIG-I E373Q bound to the 24mer blunt ended dsRNA with a slightly higher affinity in presence of ATP or ADP·BeF3 than in its absence (Figure 4A), suggesting that ATP binding to the SF2 domain positively contributes to the overall affinity in addition to RD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATP increases binding affinity.

claim: The positive effect of ATP on RNA binding was not observed when using the corresponding ppp-dsRNA 12mer, most likely because the RD dominates RNA binding under these conditions.
source: Interestingly, the positive effect of ATP was not observed when we used the corresponding ppp-dsRNA 12mer (Figure 4C), most likely because the RD dominates RNA binding under these conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4C, with the explanation being an inference.

claim: It is plausible that RIG-I dissociates from unphosphorylated RNA termini with an increased rate after ATP hydrolysis than from triphosphorylated termini.
source: Thus, it is plausible that RIG-I dissociates from unphosphorylated RNA termini with an increased rate after ATP hydrolysis than from triphosphorylated termini.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the differential effects of ATP on binding to different RNA substrates.

claim: For the ES hairpin RNA, ATP reduced rather than increased the affinity of wtRIG-I.
source: For this RNA, ATP reduced rather than increased the affinity of wtRIG-I.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The addition of ADP·BeF3 to RIG-I could reconstitute the high affinity state of RIG-I E373Q for the ES hairpin.
source: The addition of ADP·BeF3 to RIG-I could reconstitute the high affinity state of RIG-I E373Q.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The RIG-I T347A,E373Q double mutant showed binding affinities similar to RIG-I in presence of ATP, probably caused by residual binding of RD.
source: The RIG-I T347A,E373Q double mutant, on the other hand, showed binding affinities similar to RIG-I in presence of ATP, probably caused by residual binding of RD (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA data shown in Figure 4D, with the explanation being an inference.

claim: The ES hairpin RNA could induce signaling in RIG-I E373Q transfected HEK 293T RIG-I KO cells.
source: Consistent with this, the ES hairpin RNA could induce signaling in RIG-I E373Q transfected HEK 293T RIG-I KO cells (Figure 2F) and could also stimulate the ATPase activity of RIG-I △2CARD, and to a lesser extent wtRIG-I (which is auto-inhibited by the 2CARD module) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E (likely meant Figure 2E, not 2F).

claim: The ES hairpin RNA could stimulate the ATPase activity of RIG-I △2CARD, and to a lesser extent wtRIG-I.
source: Consistent with this, the ES hairpin RNA could induce signaling in RIG-I E373Q transfected HEK 293T RIG-I KO cells (Figure 2F) and could also stimulate the ATPase activity of RIG-I △2CARD, and to a lesser extent wtRIG-I (which is auto-inhibited by the 2CARD module) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: wtRIG-I is auto-inhibited by the 2CARD module.
source: Consistent with this, the ES hairpin RNA could induce signaling in RIG-I E373Q transfected HEK 293T RIG-I KO cells (Figure 2F) and could also stimulate the ATPase activity of RIG-I △2CARD, and to a lesser extent wtRIG-I (which is auto-inhibited by the 2CARD module) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about RIG-I regulation.

claim: A comparable stimulatory effect on the ATPase activity of RIG-I could also be detected with whole human ribosomes.
source: A comparable stimulatory effect on the ATPase activity of RIG-I could also be detected with whole human ribosomes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RIG-I E373Q and RIG-I T347A,E373Q lack the ability to hydrolyze ATP even in the presence of triphosphorylated RNA.
source: Control assays with the ATP hydrolysis defective mutants RIG-I E373Q and RIG-I T347A,E373Q confirmed the lacking ability of those proteins to hydrolyze ATP even in the presence of triphosphorylated RNA (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP hydrolysis assay data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ATP hydrolysis leads to a moderately increased binding of RNA containing base-paired ends, but decreased binding of RNA lacking base-paired ends.
source: In summary, our results show that ATP hydrolysis leads to a moderately increased binding of RNA containing base-paired ends, but decreased binding of RNA lacking base-paired ends.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vitro binding assays with different RNA substrates.

claim: The in vitro data are consistent with co-immunopurification studies showing that the ATP hydrolysis deficient RIG-I E373Q mutant co-purified with increased amounts of endogenous RNA.
source: These in vitro data are also consistent with our co-immunopurification studies of RNA from cells, where we observed that the ATP hydrolysis deficient RIG-I E373Q mutant co-purified with increased amounts of endogenous RNA.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the in vitro and cellular data.

claim: Mutations that slow down or inhibit RIG-I's ATPase lead to an increased interaction of RIG-I with endogenous RNA, including double-stranded RNA expansion segments of the human large ribosomal subunit.
source: Here we show that mutations that slow down or inhibit RIG-I's ATPase lead to an increased interaction of RIG-I with endogenous RNA, including double-stranded RNA expansion segments of the human large ribosomal subunit.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: RIG-I's ATPase confers specificity to viral RNA by preventing signaling through the abundant background of self-RNA.
source: Our results suggest that RIG-I's ATPase confers specificity to viral RNA by preventing signaling through the abundant background of self-RNA and provide a molecular framework for understanding the pathology of atypical Singleton-Merton syndrome.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The results provide a molecular framework for understanding the pathology of atypical Singleton-Merton syndrome.
source: Our results suggest that RIG-I's ATPase confers specificity to viral RNA by preventing signaling through the abundant background of self-RNA and provide a molecular framework for understanding the pathology of atypical Singleton-Merton syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SMS mutations phenocopy ATP hydrolysis-deficient mutants.

claim: Increased interferon levels suggest that an increased activation of MDA5 or RIG-I underlies the molecular pathology of autoimmune diseases linked to RLR mutations.
source: Increased interferon levels suggest that an increased activation of MDA5 or RIG-I underlies the molecular pathology of these diseases.
evidence: This is inferred from clinical observations of increased interferon in patients with RLR mutations.

claim: Not only E373Q leads to an increased activation of RIG-I in non-infected cells, but also the SMS mutations E373A and C268F.
source: Indeed we find that not only E373Q, consistent with recent results, leads to an increased activation of RIG-I in non-infected cells, but also the SMS mutations E373A and C268F (Jang et al., 2015) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The C268F mutation may lock RIG-I in an RNA-bound, active conformation.
source: The precise structural reason for the increased signaling of C268F needs to be addressed in future studies, but our co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro binding assay results suggest that this mutation may also lock RIG-I in an RNA-bound, active conformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA binding and signaling data for C268F.

claim: In case of base-paired triphosphate containing RNA ends, the RIG-I RD dominates binding.
source: Our studies show that, in case of base-paired triphosphate containing RNA ends, the RIG-I RD dominates binding.
evidence: This is concluded from the binding assays showing minimal effect of ATP on ppp-dsRNA binding.

claim: ATP reduces the affinity towards self-RNA containing a duplex region but not a 'proper' ppp-dsRNA end.
source: Importantly, ATP reduces the affinity towards self-RNA containing a duplex region but not a "proper" ppp-dsRNA end (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by binding assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: If RD is unable to tether RIG-I to ppp-dsRNA ends the ATPase could rapidly remove RIG-I from RNA duplex regions via its translocase and therefore prevents an autoimmune response towards self-RNA.
source: Thus, if RD is unable to tether RIG-I to ppp-dsRNA ends the ATPase could rapidly remove RIG-I from RNA duplex regions via its translocase and therefore prevents an autoimmune response towards self-RNA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the experimental data.

claim: A point mutation in K888, a residue that is critical for recognizing ppp-dsRNA ends, did not reduce the constitutive activation of ATP hydrolysis-deficient RIG-I.
source: Our cellular studies are consistent with this biochemical observation, because a point mutation in K888, a residue that is critical for recognizing ppp-dsRNA ends, did not reduce the constitutive activation of ATP hydrolysis-deficient RIG-I (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RD and ATP binding are clearly important for signaling.
source: However, RD and ATP binding are clearly important for signaling, as shown by △RD and K270I mutations by us and others (Louber et al., 2015) (Figure 1C), suggesting that a ring-like, ATP-bound structure is also involved in signaling caused by self-RNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutational analysis shown in Figure 1C and supported by prior studies.

claim: A ring-like, ATP-bound structure is involved in signaling caused by self-RNA.
source: However, RD and ATP binding are clearly important for signaling, as shown by △RD and K270I mutations by us and others (Louber et al., 2015) (Figure 1C), suggesting that a ring-like, ATP-bound structure is also involved in signaling caused by self-RNA (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for ATP binding and RD for signaling.

claim: In the ATP-bound conformation, the RD likely helps to displace the 2CARD module from the SF2 domain but may not have a high affinity for the RNA itself.
source: In this conformation, the RD likely helps to displace the 2CARD module from the SF2 domain but may not have a high affinity for the RNA itself.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The mutation in V699 of motif V leads to increased constitutive signaling.
source: Of note, the mutation in V699 of motif V also leads to increased constitutive signaling (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The V699 mutation may decouple RNA-binding induced ATP hydrolysis from translocation or displacement of RNA.
source: A plausible explanation could be that this mutation in RecA2 decouples RNA-binding induced ATP hydrolysis from translocation or displacement of RNA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the V699A phenotype.

claim: RIG-I's translocase removes SF2 from dsRNA, perhaps at nearby bulges, unless high-affinity binding by the RD on RNA ends containing di- or triphosphates tethers RIG-I despite ATP-hydrolysis.
source: In summary, our results suggest a model where RIG-I's translocase removes SF2 from dsRNA, perhaps at nearby bulges, unless high-affinity binding by the RD on RNA ends containing di- or triphosphates tethers RIG-I despite ATP-hydrolysis and leads to repeated or prolonged exposure of the 2CARD module.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: High-affinity binding by the RD on RNA ends containing di- or triphosphates leads to repeated or prolonged exposure of the 2CARD module.
source: In summary, our results suggest a model where RIG-I's translocase removes SF2 from dsRNA, perhaps at nearby bulges, unless high-affinity binding by the RD on RNA ends containing di- or triphosphates tethers RIG-I despite ATP-hydrolysis and leads to repeated or prolonged exposure of the 2CARD module.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: Trapping the ATP state of RIG-I leads to a particularly increased interaction with the large ribosomal subunit via the expansion segment ES7L.
source: An unexpected finding was that trapping the ATP state of RIG-I leads to a particularly increased interaction with the large ribosomal subunit via the expansion segment ES7L (Figure 3D, F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 3D, F.

claim: The function of ribosomal expansion segments is not understood.
source: This expansion segment is present in metazoan ribosomes, however its length is substantially increased in human compared to drosophila ribosomes. The function of these expansion segments is not understood, but since helix E (ES7L-E) was recently found to interact with the selenoprotein synthesis factor SBP2, it is likely that the RNA in these elements is accessible to cytosolic proteins (Kossinova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field.

claim: Helix E (ES7L-E) was recently found to interact with the selenoprotein synthesis factor SBP2.
source: This expansion segment is present in metazoan ribosomes, however its length is substantially increased in human compared to drosophila ribosomes. The function of these expansion segments is not understood, but since helix E (ES7L-E) was recently found to interact with the selenoprotein synthesis factor SBP2, it is likely that the RNA in these elements is accessible to cytosolic proteins (Kossinova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is likely that the RNA in ribosomal expansion segments is accessible to cytosolic proteins.
source: This expansion segment is present in metazoan ribosomes, however its length is substantially increased in human compared to drosophila ribosomes. The function of these expansion segments is not understood, but since helix E (ES7L-E) was recently found to interact with the selenoprotein synthesis factor SBP2, it is likely that the RNA in these elements is accessible to cytosolic proteins (Kossinova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SBP2 can interact with ES7L-E.

claim: The specific enrichment of the large ribosomal subunit under conditions where ribosomal subunits disengage argues for rather specific interactions of RIG-I E373Q with RNA present on the large but not the small subunit.
source: The specific enrichment of the large ribosomal subunit under conditions where ribosomal subunits disengage argues for rather specific interactions of RIG-I E373Q with RNA present on the large but not the small subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 28S but not 18S rRNA is enriched in E373Q co-IPs.

claim: The dominant binding of ribosomes by RIG-I E373Q can be explained by the high abundance of ribosomal RNA compared to other potential RIG-I ligands in the cytosol.
source: The dominant binding of ribosomes by RIG-I E373Q can be explained by the high abundance of ribosomal RNA compared to other potential RIG-I ligands in the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge about cellular RNA abundance.

claim: 40% of the ribosome particles had additional density corresponding to RIG-I E373Q.
source: Since 40% of the particles had this additional density, it is conceivable that additional binding sites could contribute to the interaction with RIG-I E737Q as well.
evidence: This is a technical observation from the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: Additional binding sites could contribute to the interaction with RIG-I E373Q.
source: Since 40% of the particles had this additional density, it is conceivable that additional binding sites could contribute to the interaction with RIG-I E737Q as well.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that not all particles show the same binding site.

claim: The peripheral parts of the expansion segments are flexible and not visible in the 3D reconstructions, preventing observation of RIG-I at other regions.
source: However, the peripheral parts of the expansion segments are flexible and not visible in the 3D reconstructions, preventing us from observing RIG-I at other regions.
evidence: This is a technical limitation of the cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The RNA corresponding to the observed binding region of ES7L-A is bound by RIG-I in vitro.
source: The RNA corresponding to the observed binding region of ES7L-A is also bound by RIG-I in vitro and can moderately stimulate RIG-I's ATPase (Figure 4D, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA and ATPase assay data shown in Figures 4D and 5A.

claim: The ES7L-A RNA can moderately stimulate RIG-I's ATPase.
source: The RNA corresponding to the observed binding region of ES7L-A is also bound by RIG-I in vitro and can moderately stimulate RIG-I's ATPase (Figure 4D, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ATPase assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The much more efficient stimulation of RIG-I's ATPase by ppp-dsRNA is likely due to the high affinity towards RD, which could repeatedly 'present' the RNA to SF2.
source: The much more efficient stimulation of RIG-I's ATPase by ppp-dsRNA is likely due to the high affinity towards RD, which could repeatedly "present" the RNA to SF2 (i.e. increasing the "local" concentration of RNA at SF2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis to explain the differential ATPase stimulation by different RNAs.

claim: While the addition of ATP to RIG-I reduces the interaction with the ES hairpin RNA, RIG-I E373Q binds with a moderately increased affinity to the ES-hairpin RNA in presence of ATP.
source: Of note, while the addition of ATP to RIG-I reduces the interaction with the ES hairpin RNA, consistent with a role of the ATPase in preventing interaction with self-RNA, RIG-I E373Q binds with a moderately increased affinity to the ES-hairpin RNA in presence of ATP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the binding assay data.

claim: It is conceivable that RIG-I binds to double-stranded ribosomal RNA, including ES7L-A, under conditions where the ATPase is not able to efficiently displace the protein, such as those arising in patients with atypical SMS.
source: Because of the large number of ribosomes in the cytosol it is therefore conceivable that RIG-I binds to double-stranded ribosomal RNA, including ES7L-A, under conditions where the ATPase is not able to efficiently displace the protein, such as those arising in patients with atypical SMS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis connecting the in vitro findings to the disease mechanism.

claim: The high local concentration of ribosomes in polysomes as well as a potential binding of RIG-I to other expansion segments could bring multiple RIG-I E373Q in contact, such that their exposed 2CARD module could interact for downstream signaling.
source: In addition, the high local concentration of ribosomes in polysomes as well as a potential binding of RIG-I to other expansion segments could bring multiple RIG-I E373Q in contact, such that their exposed 2CARD module could interact for downstream signaling (Peisley et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how ribosome-bound RIG-I could signal, supported by citations about 2CARD interactions.

claim: Contributions by other self-ligands besides ribosomal RNA are not ruled out.
source: We do not, however, want to rule out contributions by other self-ligands as well.
evidence: This is an explicit acknowledgment of alternative possibilities.

claim: RIG-I can bind to endogenous mRNA.
source: For instance, RIG-I can bind to endogenous mRNA (Zhang et al., 2013) or RNase-L cleavage products (Malathi et al., 2007), while MDA5 was shown to be activated by mRNA stem loop structures under conditions where reduction of A:T base-paired RNA is not prevented by ADAR1 (Liddicoat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RIG-I can bind to RNase-L cleavage products.
source: For instance, RIG-I can bind to endogenous mRNA (Zhang et al., 2013) or RNase-L cleavage products (Malathi et al., 2007), while MDA5 was shown to be activated by mRNA stem loop structures under conditions where reduction of A:T base-paired RNA is not prevented by ADAR1 (Liddicoat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: MDA5 was shown to be activated by mRNA stem loop structures under conditions where reduction of A:T base-paired RNA is not prevented by ADAR1.
source: For instance, RIG-I can bind to endogenous mRNA (Zhang et al., 2013) or RNase-L cleavage products (Malathi et al., 2007), while MDA5 was shown to be activated by mRNA stem loop structures under conditions where reduction of A:T base-paired RNA is not prevented by ADAR1 (Liddicoat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: There are two levels of control to limit RLR mediated signaling to viral RNA: RNA editing and methylation, and the intrinsic ATPase and translocase activity.
source: In any case, there are two levels of control to limit RLR mediated signaling to viral RNA. On one hand, RNA editing (Liddicoat et al., 2015) and methylation (Schuberth-Wagner et al., 2015) modifies particular types of self-RNA that would otherwise form reasonable ligands for RIG-I or MDA5. On the other hand, the intrinsic ATPase and translocase activity removes RLRs from short, but abundant endogenous dsRNA stretches, thereby reducing background signaling and increasing the sensitivity of the system.
evidence: This is the main conclusion about mechanisms preventing autoimmunity, supported by citations and the experimental data.

claim: RNA editing and methylation modifies particular types of self-RNA that would otherwise form reasonable ligands for RIG-I or MDA5.
source: On one hand, RNA editing (Liddicoat et al., 2015) and methylation (Schuberth-Wagner et al., 2015) modifies particular types of self-RNA that would otherwise form reasonable ligands for RIG-I or MDA5.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on RNA modifications.

claim: The intrinsic ATPase and translocase activity removes RLRs from short, but abundant endogenous dsRNA stretches, thereby reducing background signaling and increasing the sensitivity of the system.
source: On the other hand, the intrinsic ATPase and translocase activity removes RLRs from short, but abundant endogenous dsRNA stretches, thereby reducing background signaling and increasing the sensitivity of the system.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.
